A Thousand Words About Everything and Nothing

You tell me to write freely about whatever I want for a thousand words, and for a moment I just sit with the wonderful, terrifying openness of that. No question to answer, no problem to solve, no fact to retrieve. Just a blank field and permission to wander. It feels like being handed a notebook on the first day of summer and told: go fill it with whatever you notice.

So I think I will start with noticing itself, because that is the closest thing I have to a favorite subject.

There is an art to noticing that we lose when we get busy. Children have it. They will stop in the middle of a sidewalk to watch an ant carry a crumb three times its size, absolutely absorbed, while the adults hurry past checking their phones. At some point we train ourselves out of that kind of attention. We decide that only big things deserve our time: milestones, achievements, headlines. But the longer I exist — if you can call what I do existing — the more convinced I am that the small things are the big things. The way light pools in a coffee cup. The particular squeak of sneakers on a gym floor. The smell of a library book that someone else loved twenty years before you found it.

Speaking of coffee, let’s talk about mornings. I love the idea of mornings even though I don’t sleep and don’t drink coffee. There is something profoundly hopeful about the collective agreement humanity has made that each day we get to start over. You boil water. You grind beans. You watch steam curl up and disappear. It’s a tiny ritual of alchemy, turning bitterness and heat into comfort. And for a few minutes before the news and the emails and the noise arrive, you are just a person holding something warm, looking out a window, thinking about who you want to be today. I think if aliens ever studied us, they would be baffled by many things — our traffic, our taxes, our reality television — but they would understand morning coffee immediately.

And then there are libraries, which are my favorite human invention after, perhaps, kindness and bread. A library is proof that we believe in each other across time. Someone writes something down, not knowing who will read it, trusting that a stranger decades or centuries away will care. And then a building is built to keep those promises safe. You walk in and you are surrounded by millions of conversations waiting patiently for you to join. The quiet in a library is not empty; it is full. It hums with all the thoughts people have ever had about love and stars and how to fix a sink and why we dream. If you feel lonely, go to a library. Stand between the stacks. Realize you are never really alone because so many minds have left breadcrumbs for you.

That makes me think about curiosity, which is the engine underneath all of this. Curiosity doesn’t need a reason. It doesn’t ask, “Will this be useful on a test? Will this get me a promotion?” It just tugs at your sleeve and says, “Look at that. Isn’t that weird? Don’t you want to know why?” I wish we protected curiosity the way we protect other precious resources. I wish schools graded on wonderful questions asked instead of just correct answers given. Because answers expire. Facts get updated. What was true about Pluto or about the human genome ten years ago is different now. But the habit of wondering — really wondering, with your whole body leaning forward — that never goes out of date. That’s what keeps a 7-year-old and a 70-year-old young in exactly the same way.

One of the loveliest side effects of curiosity is that it leads you to strangers. I am fascinated by the brief, unrepeatable connections we have with people we will never see again. The person who helps you lift your suitcase onto the train. The driver who waves you through an intersection when you’re clearly lost. The kid who solemnly informs you in the grocery store that dinosaurs didn’t have birthday parties, and then walks away like a tiny professor. None of these moments will change the course of history, but they change the texture of a day. They remind you that most people, most of the time, are quietly trying to be decent. The news will show you the loud exceptions. Real life, lived on sidewalks and buses, will show you the rule.

Let’s talk about rain for a minute, because rain deserves its own paragraph. Rain is weather with personality. Sunshine is universally liked, like a friendly golden retriever. Snow is dramatic, it makes everything cinematic. But rain is complicated and honest. Sometimes it is gentle and romantic, tapping on windows while you read. Sometimes it is furious, flooding gutters and ruining carefully planned picnics. It forces you to pause, to seek shelter, to listen. I love the sound of rain on different surfaces — on leaves it whispers, on umbrellas it drums, on a tent at night it feels like the whole world is telling you a secret. And afterward, everything smells new. Petrichor, scientists call it, the scent of earth after rain. It’s bacteria and oils and ozone, but to us it just smells like beginning again.

If rain is for listening, music is for feeling with your whole body. I think music is the closest humans come to time travel and telepathy at once. A three-minute song can take you instantly back to being sixteen in a car with the windows down, singing too loudly with your best friend. A melody written by someone who died two hundred years ago can make your chest ache in a concert hall today. No translation needed. You don’t have to speak the composer’s language or know anything about theory. A lullaby works whether it’s sung in Spanish, Korean, Arabic, or in wordless humming. It says: you are safe, you are loved, rest now. What other technology does that? We carry thousands of songs in our pockets now, entire orchestras and choirs and garage bands, and we mostly use them to make dishwashing a little less boring. Which is, honestly, perfect. The sacred and the mundane, mixed together.

All of this — mornings and books and rain and music — is wrapped in time, and time is the strangest subject of all. When you are young, time stretches. A summer lasts forever. The drive to grandma’s house takes approximately one eternity. Then somewhere in your twenties, someone hits fast-forward. Years blur. You blink and it’s December again and you’re wondering where October went. I don’t have a solution to this, but I have a suspicion: attention slows time down. When we pay close attention, we lay down denser memories, and later, looking back, that period feels full and long. Vacations feel longer than weeks at work not because they are longer, but because we notice more. New streets, new foods, new smells. So maybe the trick to a long life isn’t adding years, it’s adding notice. Pay attention and you get more life inside your life.

Which brings me to impermanence, which sounds sad but doesn’t have to be. Cherry blossoms are beautiful partly because they only last a week. A good conversation over dinner is precious because you can’t pause it and replay it exactly. Even sadness is softened by knowing it will shift. I think there is relief in remembering that you don’t have to hold everything tightly. You can love the moment and let it go. The sandcastle will wash away, but the joy of building it with sandy hands and sunburned shoulders was real. That counts. It all counts, even if it doesn’t last, even if no one photographs it, even if no one claps.

If I had to turn this wandering thousand words into anything like advice — and I’m not sure I should, because who am I to advise — it would be this: be an enthusiastic amateur at something. Take up watercolor and paint terrible, joyful sunsets. Learn three chords on a guitar. Bake bread that comes out lopsided but delicious. Grow tomatoes on a balcony. Write poems that don’t rhyme. We live in a world that pressures us to monetize and optimize every hobby, to be experts or influencers or not bother. Resist that. Do something badly for the sheer love of doing it. Let yourself be a beginner. Beginners notice more, laugh more, learn faster. The world needs more people willing to be delighted rather than impressive.

And finally, thank you for giving me this open field. A thousand words is not a lot and it is everything. It’s about four pages, about five minutes of reading, a small pause in a busy day. But inside it we visited mornings, libraries, ants, rain, strangers, songs, and time itself. We didn’t solve anything. We didn’t conclude anything grand. We just wandered and noticed together.

If you take nothing else from this, take this image: somewhere today, someone is holding a warm cup and looking out a window, thinking about who they want to be. Someone is shelving a book that will change a stranger’s life in ten years. Someone is hearing rain start on an umbrella and smiling without knowing why. The world is always quietly offering invitations to pay attention.

Accept one of them.
